about: Figures for promotion: candorlanguage.org reads this file, and the README's Numbers section once it has one. `language` and each trial's `results` are filled in by `bun run numbers`; the rest is written by hand. Every claim carries its catches, so nothing says more than was measured.

headline.how: Opus, one frozen Candor version, Go as the only baseline, on five new apps never used to tune the docs. Specs, requests and hidden tests are committed before any run, and the results are published as they stand.

numbers.title: Changes accepted first time
numbers.what: One run, no questions asked: every hidden test passes, no shared test breaks, and a refactor keeps the shape asked for.

numbers.title: Cost per accepted change
numbers.what: What all of a language's runs cost, divided by the changes accepted, at API prices.

numbers.title: Side-effect questions answered
numbers.what: Given a diff and its codebase, what side effects does the change add? Scored against a known answer, with the tokens it took.

numbers.title: Cost to write a new app
numbers.what: One run per app from a spec, at API prices. The model knows Go, and learns Candor from its docs in the run.

stages.title: Build the five new apps, in both languages

headline.later: Passes two and three repeat the change requests and the review, as the budget allows.
catches: None of these figures come from the new trial. Their apps and requests were also used while tuning Candor's docs; the new trial's five apps won't be.
In the change trial Go's codebases were written by people and Candor's were ported by a model, which may suit a model reading them. In the new trial a model writes both.

The Opus figures are from Candor 0.0.29 with one run per request, so a single miss would move a pass rate by a quarter. The Sonnet figures are from a later version, and the two languages ran on different days.
Dollars are the API-equivalent cost Claude Code reports, not what a subscription charges.

trials.title: Same spec, Candor and Go
trials.how: One headless run per app and language from the same spec, no questions asked; hidden acceptance tests check the build. The model learns Candor from its docs, in the run.
catches: Candor pays a reading cost Go doesn't: the model knows Go, and learns Candor from its docs in the run. Before writing code, Candor runs read the guide (docs/agent.md and its service part, about 14 thousand characters; the two that need concurrency read agent-more.md too), the heads of the std modules they use and sometimes an example; Go runs read the spec. That is most of the gap in context and in tokens. A whole service in agent-more.md (2026-10-30) cut the median context from 27k to 24k and the Candor cost from $1.95 to $1.47; on 0.0.30 (2026-10-31) it was 23k and $1.40. The http and json signatures and a shutdown pattern beside that service (2026-10-31) took most of the http and start.md lookups away but made the guide longer by about as much: 22k and $1.47. Moving the service into a part of its own (2026-10-31), so runs writing a service skip concurrency, tests and the std map, gave 20.5k and $1.41: 5 of 6 apps read less, by up to 5k; one run each, so about the noise. The Candor runs here are from 2026-10-31, Go's from 2026-10-29.
Candor runs wrote fewer lines on four apps of six, tests included, and ran the compiler as often or more: 3 to 8 times, Go 2 to 5.
One run per app and language: a small sample. Minutes are wall time on a machine shared with other work.
The 2026-10-26 runs on Kimi Code (Candor 0.0.1) stay in trials/runs, unlisted.

compare.title: Other agents on the change trial
compare.how: Its four change requests, Go and Candor, one headless run each per agent and model (sonnet: the change trial's three from before the shorter guide, the docs the other agents had), scored as in the change trial.
catches: Every agent passed every request in both languages, and every agent had taken in more context by its first Candor edit than by its first Go one: sonnet 1.4 times, Opus 1.7, Gemini 1.6. The gap is the language's (or its docs'), not one model's.
Gemini through Antigravity reads about three times what Claude Code does before its first edit, in both languages; its own setup is about the same size (8k), so that is reading.
Tokens in all are Candor's widest gap for Opus and Gemini (about 3 times Go's), mostly cached reads over longer runs: more turns and compiler runs in Candor. Sonnet's runs stayed short in both.
One run per request and language for Opus and Gemini: a single miss would move a pass rate by a quarter. Antigravity reports no cost; Opus cost $3.07 for 8 runs, sonnet $2.25 for 24.

Antigravity runs headless with an allowlist of its file and shell tools (any path: its rules take an exact path or `*`) and its sandbox. One Gemini run was dropped and run again: the sandbox failed to start a process, and the agent stopped.

change.title: Changing a codebase, Go and Candor
change.how: Three headless runs per request and language, no questions asked; hidden tests, the shared tests and, for a refactor, a shape check score the change.

ntfy.what: pub/sub notification server: HTTP, SQLite, users and ACLs, rate limits

webhook.what: runs commands on HTTP hooks: trigger rules, payloads, signatures

supercronic.what: cron for containers: schedules, time zones, child processes

ntfy/acl-bug.what: a specific grant overruled by a broader one

ntfy/user-limits.what: rate limits per user, not per IP

ntfy/priority-type.what: message priority gets a type of its own

webhook/max-concurrent.what: a per-hook limit on running commands

webhook/whitelist-bug.what: an address refused unless its range comes first

webhook/typed-match.what: a match rule's type decided when the file is read

supercronic/job-names.what: name a job with a `# name:` comment

supercronic/env-bug.what: an env value with `=` in it cut short

supercronic/exit-code.what: a failed job's exit code as a log field

supercronic/options-struct.what: one options value instead of loose flags

catches: Minutes are measured on a machine shared with other heavy work; read them as rough.

Go's runs are from 2026-10-28 night; Candor's were run again on 2026-10-31 on Candor 0.0.30 (#b62264d5), with tests in their own files and the two-part guide. Go doesn't read Candor's docs. Candor's median context at the first edit stayed at 17k (20k on 0.0.29's first runs), Go's is 14k; its tokens in all fell from 155k to 133k, under Go's 164k.
The Go codebases are idiomatic code by their authors; the Candor ones are ports written by a model, which may suit a model reading them.
Three runs per request and language is still a small sample; the spread is shown, not hidden.

Pass rates hardly separate the languages: 36 of 39 Go runs and all 39 Candor runs passed (37 of 39 on 0.0.29). Context is where they differ: Candor's first edit came later in reading on 7 requests of 13 (more than a tenth later), about as early on 5, earlier on 1.

topic-limits was once the widest gap (35k against 27k), and it was the codebase: the Candor port had left out the topic registry Go's ntfy has, so its runs built one first. With the registry added to the port and topic-limits rerun, it is even. Every Candor run also reads agent.md, about 2k tokens. The widest gaps left (max-concurrent, exit-code, options-struct) are equal work where Candor's way takes more: shared state as a Mutex field of the server, a declared error type in place of Go's wrapped errors, and a bigger test suite in the port. Summing every call's input, as an earlier figure here did, counted early reads again on every call; the dollar gap is smaller still, since cached reads are billed at a tenth.

ports.what: HTTP endpoints that run commands: hook rules, payload matching, HMAC signatures, timeouts.
ports.how: Ported from the Go source, headless, no questions asked; the original's tests ported with it.

passes.note: Worked around what Candor lacked: its own regex engine, HMAC-SHA1 by hand.
Workarounds dropped once Candor had regex and HMAC; served real requests, a timeout killed a slow command.
Payload numbers (`1.50`, `1e3`, `12345678901234567890`) reach the command exactly as sent, as in the original.

catches: Trailing data after a JSON body is an error; Go ignores it.
Multipart, XML and some flags left out of scope.
Three Candor releases between the passes: the port drove the language as much as it tested it.

ports.what: An RSS reader: JSON API, SQLite with 15 migrations, background refresh, RSS, Atom, RDF and JSON Feed parsing, an HTML sanitizer.
ports.how: Ported from the Go source, headless, no questions asked; all 29 of the original's parser fixtures and 38 sanitizer cases ported with it.

passes.note: Before Candor had XML. Found a page's feed, served its items, got a 304 on refresh.
With std `xml`: its own XML reader and charset tables dropped; fixtures unchanged, same output.

catches: It still has its own HTML tree builder and URL resolver.
Its search index differs from the original's: Candor has no SQL functions.

ownApps.what: of the author's own apps, rewritten in Candor and in daily use; one of them reads and sends mail over IMAP and SMTP.
